To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

new mutations in Arabidosis thaliana are equally as likely to decrease as increase fitness components in the field, and that new mutations are more likely to decrease a trait when tested under stressful field conditions than benign artificial conditions.

(1) new mutations are equally likely to increase or decrease traits not related to fitness, (2) new mutations are more likely to decrease traits related to fitness under stressful than benign conditions, and (3) the effects of new mutation on traits not related to survival or reproduction do not differ between benign and stressful conditions.

new mutations in Arabidosis thaliana are more likely to decrease traits that contribute directly to fitness when measured in the field than in the laboratory, and are equally as likely to decrease as increase fitness‐related traits as well as nonfitness‐related traits when measured in the laboratory.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of mutations in generating variation in natural populations.
the role of mutation in the evolution of natural populations and how mutation effects are influenced by the environment in which the mutations are measured.
the effects of new genetic mutations on fitness components and other traits.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of new mutation is not uniform across traits or environments.

mutations are likely to be more deleterious under stressful conditions, and that mutations affecting fitness are likely to be skewed towards being deleterious, but that the effects of mutations on nonfitness traits are likely to be bidirectional and not skewed towards being deletrious.
new mutations can have a wide range of effects on fitness‐related and nonfitness traits and that these effects can vary with the environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
new mutations are more likely to have a negative impact on traits that are related to fitness and are more likely to do so under stressful conditions.
new mutations can have a wide range of effects, depending on the trait and environment in which they were tested.
new mutations have the potential to be both positive and negative in the context of fitness and fitness components, and this potential is influenced by environmental conditions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of new mutation on fitness and fitness‐related traits are likely to be more negative under more stressful conditions than under benign conditions.
the effects of induced mutations on fitness‐related traits are likely to be highly dependent on the environmental conditions in which they are assayed.
new mutations are not always deleterious, and their effects on fitness are dependent on the conditions under which they are tested.
